entities.name: Daedalus of Sicyon
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Daedalus of Sicyon, an eminent Greek sculptor of the late Classical era, flourished primarily in the mid-4th century BCE, active around 370-340 BCE. As the son of the sculptor Patrocles and a pupil of the renowned Polykleitos the Younger, Daedalus inherited and advanced the Peloponnesian sculptural tradition, particularly known for his mastery in bronze. His work, rooted in the artistic hub of Sicyon, contributed significantly to the evolving aesthetic of Greek art, bridging the high classical ideals of the 5th century with the more expressive tendencies emerging in the 4th century BCE, characterized by a refined sense of athletic form and balanced composition.

His commissions spanned important Panhellenic sanctuaries and city-states, underscoring his reputation across ancient Greece. Among his notable works, he crafted a bronze trophy for the Eleans to commemorate their victory over the Arcadians in 364 BCE, which was erected at Olympia. He also created statues of victorious athletes, a common and prestigious commission for leading sculptors of the time, including works for the Argives. These creations, while now lost and known primarily through literary accounts by Pausanias and Pliny the Elder, exemplified the technical prowess and artistic sensibility of the Sicyonian school, which emphasized precision, anatomical accuracy, and harmonious proportions in its bronze statuary.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Daedalus of Sicyon holds regional significance for his role in maintaining and subtly evolving the Peloponnesian sculptural tradition, influencing the stylistic development of 4th-century BCE Greek art through his bronze works and the Sicyonian school. His contributions are recorded by ancient authors, ensuring his place in the history of classical sculpture.
